completion_reason: Three material validation-risk decisions remain unresolved: stale output handling, dependency release gates, and resource-ceiling safety behavior.

questions.label: Late run outputs
questions.context: A late output is a result that arrives after its run attempt was canceled, timed out, or replaced by a fallback attempt. The durable run record needs one rule for whether that output can affect the accepted result.
questions.evidence: `kits/jobs-kit/index.mjs` owns cancellation, timeout, retry, idempotency, and terminal state, while `services/nexus-node/src/run-coordinator.mjs` writes canonical results and artifacts. The verified architecture does not say whether an executor response arriving after terminal state may update those records.
questions.impact: This decides whether failover can silently overwrite accepted work. It establishes the long-term consistency rule shared by direct, LAN mesh, PeerJS, and future provider transports.
questions.question: What should NexusCentral do with an output that arrives after its run attempt is already terminal?

choices.consequence: Store the late output with its attempt identity for diagnosis, but never let it change the canonical result, approval state, artifacts, or workflow memory; this costs storage but gives deterministic recovery and auditability.
Ignore the late output and store only a small late-response event; this minimizes sensitive-data retention and storage, but weakens debugging and provider accountability.
Keep the output and let an operator replace the accepted result after review; this can recover valuable work, but adds a second result-promotion path and complicates immutable run history.

questions.recommendation_reason: Preserving the response as non-authoritative evidence keeps immutable run state deterministic while retaining enough information to diagnose duplicate execution, cancellation races, and unreliable providers.

questions.label: Dependency release gate
questions.context: A dependency finding is a reported vulnerability in third-party code used by NexusCentral. A release gate determines which findings must be resolved or explicitly waived before a production build can be accepted.
questions.evidence: `docs/12-IMPLEMENTATION-STATUS.md` lists dependency-audit findings among the current release gaps even though the project target is a production-ready system. No supplied boundary defines which severity or exploitability level blocks release.
questions.impact: This sets the minimum security evidence required for every release and determines whether production acceptance is reproducible or based on ad hoc judgment.
questions.question: Which dependency findings should block production acceptance?

choices.consequence: Block known high/critical findings that affect shipped, reachable code unless a time-limited documented waiver is approved; this balances enforceable safety with practical handling of false positives and unreachable packages.
Block all high/critical findings regardless of reachability; this is simpler and stricter, but may stop releases for unused build tooling or unexploitable dependency paths.
Block only critical findings and track lower severities after release; this speeds delivery but permits known high-severity exposure into production.
Show the audit report for manual sign-off but impose no automatic threshold; this maximizes flexibility while making release safety inconsistent across operators.

questions.recommendation_reason: A reachability-aware high/critical gate protects shipped behavior without letting irrelevant transitive findings permanently deadlock releases; expiring waivers keep exceptions visible and temporary.

questions.label: Resource ceiling response
questions.context: A resource ceiling is an operator-configured limit on CPU, GPU memory, RAM, disk, network use, cost, or concurrency. The safety decision is what happens when starting or continuing work would exceed one of those limits.
questions.evidence: `kits/jobs-kit/index.mjs` owns durable queue and progress state, `kits/providers-kit/index.mjs` owns provider health, and the Models and Settings surfaces are intended to own runtime lifecycle and service controls. The verified architecture does not define a shared response when a runtime or queued job reaches a configured ceiling.
questions.impact: This determines whether overload causes data loss, host instability, or predictable backpressure. The rule will shape scheduling and runtime arbitration across all workflows and users.
questions.question: How should NexusCentral respond when a configured resource ceiling is reached?

choices.consequence: Reject new leases, let active work reach a safe checkpoint when possible, then pause it and show the blocking ceiling; this protects the host and preserves recoverability, but may delay urgent work.
Cancel or kill enough active work to return below the ceiling; this restores capacity fastest, but can waste compute and increases interrupted-run recovery risk.
Reduce concurrency or choose lighter eligible models while allowing work to proceed; this improves continuity, but may change latency or output quality and makes acceptance evidence less uniform.
Display the overage and continue unchanged until the operator intervenes; this is flexible, but ceilings cease to be dependable safety controls in unattended workflows.

questions.recommendation_reason: Blocking new starts while checkpointing active work makes ceilings enforceable without turning routine pressure into corrupted or unnecessarily lost runs.
